summary:
Rio Grande do Sul stands under Brazil's national legal framework for LGBTI people. The sources covering this state record no deviation from that framework material enough to distinguish it, so a trans visitor in Rio Grande do Sul is governed by the same rules that apply in every other Brazilian state.

Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since May 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries and was adopted in a 14-1 vote. Spousal-visa equality and joint adoption follow from the same regime, with adoption rights in place since 2015.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled in ADO 26 that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. Outright International's 2026 country overview notes that this ruling is the operative protection because no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists, and that repeal efforts have been mounted in Congress.

Legal gender recognition does not require surgery. A law-firm guide current as of 5 April 2026 confirms that name and gender-marker changes without surgery operate nationwide, alongside same-sex marriage and spousal-visa equality, so a trans visitor's documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters. The Superior Court of Justice ruled in 2023 that nonbinary people may amend their civil records.

Two gaps sit inside the protective text. Intersex people have no specific legal protections under Brazilian law. Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the military, but the protections that exist rest on a court ruling rather than on dedicated legislation.

The guide adds a distributional point that matters on the ground: larger cities carry legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction. Rio Grande do Sul's capital and interior therefore present different practical conditions even though the statute is uniform.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between the statutory position and lived experience is documented nationally. Outright International's March 2026 overview records that LGBTIQ people in Brazil still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and a May 2024 investigation documented drink-spiking robberies targeting LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo nightlife. Neither source isolates Rio Grande do Sul, so the state's own level of such incidents is not established here.

The 2019 ruling's placement inside the racism provisions gives SOGI-based discrimination a unusually high penalty tier by regional standards, but the absence of a dedicated federal statute leaves the protection dependent on judicial interpretation and exposed to the repeal efforts noted in Congress.

Case law analysed for 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward extending the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, which would bring trans people within Brazil's violence-prevention statutes. That extension is not confirmed as settled in the sources supplied.

Detention in Brazil is governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, which requires a judge to consult an arrested person about their placement preference, recognises LGBTI status by self-declaration, prohibits using LGBTI-specific units as disciplinary isolation, and bars compulsory transfer as punishment. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons found 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates held in eleven units operated as masculine, indicating that practice does not reliably follow the framework. No equivalent census for Rio Grande do Sul is in the inventory.

Residents of Rio Grande do Sul access name and gender-marker change without a surgical requirement, under the Supreme Federal Court's 2018 decision and the registry practice confirmed by the April 2026 guide. The Superior Court of Justice's 2023 ruling additionally allows nonbinary people to amend their civil records.

Marriage, joint adoption and spousal-visa sponsorship are available to same-sex couples on the same terms as different-sex couples, with adoption rights in place since 2015 and marriage governed by National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which is binding on every civil registry in the country.

Lesbian, gay and bisexual people may serve openly in the Brazilian armed forces. Intersex residents have no specific statutory protections, and the anti-discrimination protection available to LGBTI residents rests on the Supreme Federal Court's 13 June 2019 ruling rather than on a dedicated federal statute, leaving it exposed to the repeal efforts recorded in Congress as of 2026.

Residents bringing complaints of SOGI-based discrimination invoke Lei 7.716/1989 as applied by the 2019 ruling, which places the offence on the same footing as racism and carries imprisonment and fines. Residents in smaller cities and rural parts of Rio Grande do Sul face more social friction than those in larger cities, where legal infrastructure is concentrated.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports enforcement data specific to Rio Grande do Sul: there is no count of prosecutions under Lei 7.716/1989 for SOGI-based discrimination in this state, no record of state court decisions applying the 2019 ruling, and no figure for reported anti-trans incidents here. Whether the state's police and prosecutors apply the national framework as written is unresolved on the material supplied.

The inventory contains no Rio Grande do Sul data on detention placement for trans, travesti or intersex people. The only empirical census available is the April-June 2021 study of Rio de Janeiro state prisons, which cannot be read across to this state; how Resolution 348/366 is applied in Rio Grande do Sul's custodial units is not sourced.

Facilities, screening at entry, and access to gender-affirming care in Rio Grande do Sul are not covered by any source listed here. The claim that larger cities carry legal infrastructure while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction comes from a single law-firm guide and is not corroborated by state-level evidence in this inventory.

The extension of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women is described in the sources as a direction lower courts pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward in 2022; whether that extension is settled law by 2026 is not confirmed in the material supplied.
